**Service Name:** Uber US Terms of Use

**Summary:** These Terms of Service outline the agreements and relationships between you, as an Uber user, and the company, Uber. They cover various aspects, including content usage, data protection, disputes, and termination.

**Key Provisions:**

* The Terms apply to Uber's products and services listed on their official terms page.
* Uber can use your user-submitted content to operate, improve, and train its AI/ML systems, but only in accordance with your settings and applicable law. (This means they might use your data to make their services better, but will follow your chosen settings and any relevant regulations.)
* The company's **Privacy Policy** sets out what personal data they collect and how it's processed. You should check the policy for more information on this.
* **Dispute Resolution:** Most disputes will be resolved through binding arbitration (a private dispute process instead of court), with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts. This means you won't be able to take Uber to court for most issues; instead, you'll have to use a third-party arbitration service. However, if you don't opt out within 30 days of creating your account, you'll be bound by this dispute resolution process.
* **Termination:** Either you or Uber can terminate the agreement, but you should check the current live document for specific conditions.
* To seek help or ask questions, visit the company's contact page (https://www.uber.com/legal/en/document/?country=united-states&lang=en&name=general-terms-of-use).

**Clauses to Consider:**

* **Arbitration with Class-Action Waiver:** This is a binding arbitration process, which means you might not have the opportunity to take Uber to court or join a class-action lawsuit with others who have similar issues.
* **Data Use:** While Uber will use your content to make their services better, you might want to review their **Privacy Policy** to fully understand what they do with your data.
* **Termination:** Check the current live document for specific conditions on terminating the agreement with Uber.
* **Dispute Resolution Window:** If you have concerns or disputes, be sure to opt out of arbitration within the 30-day window for new accounts to try alternative dispute resolution.

These Terms of Service aim to outline the mutual agreements between you and Uber. However, some clauses might have implications for your rights and freedoms. Be sure to review the document carefully and understand your obligations and responsibilities within the service.
source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — UBER US TERMS OF USE (Effective 2024; replaces the 2023 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Uber and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2024 version differs from the 2023 version in the following ways: 2024 update revised arbitration after the New Jersey Uber Eats arbitration decision, added language on AI-generated trip summaries and driver/rider safety features, and expanded liability sections regarding third-party services.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Uber to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://www.uber.com/legal/en/document/?country=united-states&lang=en&name=general-terms-of-use . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20230101000000*/https://www.uber.com/legal/en/document/?country=united-states&lang=en&name=general-terms-of-use .

**Airbnb Terms of Service Summary**

The service name is the Airbnb Terms of Service, which governs the relationship between you and Airbnb and applies to the products and services described on their official terms page.

**Key Provisions**

* **Scope**: These terms cover your use of Airbnb's services, products, and features.
* **Content and License**: Airbnb can use your submitted content, such as photos and reviews, to operate, improve, and train their AI systems, subject to your settings and applicable law.
* **Privacy**: Your personal data is protected by Airbnb's published Privacy Policy, which explains how your data is collected and processed.
* **Dispute Resolution**: Most users, including you, will have to use binding arbitration (a private dispute process instead of court) to resolve disputes with Airbnb. Class-action lawsuits are not allowed. However, users with "Steam (Valve)" accounts are exempt from mandatory arbitration.
* **Termination**: Either Airbnb or you can terminate the agreement under certain conditions described in the live document.

**Harmful Clauses to Be Aware of**

* **Mandatory Arbitration**: The Terms of Service require most users to use binding arbitration to resolve disputes with Airbnb, which may limit your access to a court judgment.
* **Class-Action Waiver**: The Terms of Service prohibit class-action lawsuits, which can make it harder for users to hold Airbnb accountable for widespread issues.

**Important: Review and Understand**

It's essential to review the full Terms of Service document and the linked Privacy Policy to understand how your data is used and what rights you have. If you're unsure about specific provisions, feel free to ask.
source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — AIRBNB TERMS OF SERVICE (Effective 2024; replaces the 2023 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Airbnb and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2024 version differs from the 2023 version in the following ways: 2024 update added new AnyWhere/Icons experience terms, revised cancellation and refund policies (including AirCover updates), added language on automated/AI-driven listing detection (e.g. anti-party tools), and updated arbitration provisions.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Airbnb to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://www.airbnb.com/help/article/2908 . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20230101000000*/https://www.airbnb.com/help/article/2908 .

The service name is Cloudflare Self-Serve Subscription Agreement.

Here's a plain-language summary:

Cloudflare offers a range of products and services, and these updated Terms of Service govern how you interact with them. Key provisions of the agreement include:

* **Scope**: These terms cover your relationship with Cloudflare and apply to the products and services listed on their official terms page.
* **Content and License**: Cloudflare uses user-submitted content to improve and train its AI/ML systems, but this only happens subject to your settings and applicable law.
* **Privacy**: The terms cross-reference Cloudflare's published Privacy Policy, which explains the types of personal data collected and how it's processed.
* **Dispute Resolution**: Most provisions require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, meaning you can't join a group lawsuit. You have a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts if you don't want this process.
* **Termination**: Either Cloudflare or you can terminate the agreement under specific conditions.

Things to be aware of:

* **Anti-scraping and AI-bot abuse rules** are now stronger in the 2024 version, which may affect how you use the service.
* You agree that customer prompts/outputs in Workers AI are not used to train Cloudflare's models.
* The termination clause allows Cloudflare to end the agreement subject to certain conditions.

Please note that these summaries and explanations are based on the provided Terms of Service, but should not be considered professional legal advice.
source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — CLOUDFLARE SELF-SERVE SUBSCRIPTION AGREEMENT (Effective 2024; replaces the 2023 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Cloudflare and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2024 version differs from the 2023 version in the following ways: 2024 update added AI Gateway and Workers AI specific terms, clarified that customer prompts/outputs in Workers AI are not used to train Cloudflare's models, and revised acceptable-use rules with stronger anti-scraping/AI-bot abuse language.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Cloudflare to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://www.cloudflare.com/terms/ . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20230101000000*/https://www.cloudflare.com/terms/ .

**Key Provisions:**

* **Scope:** These terms apply to all Stripe products and services listed on their official terms page.

To learn more about these terms, you can visit Stripe's official website at [https://stripe.com/legal/ssa](https://stripe.com/legal/ssa).
source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — STRIPE SERVICES AGREEMENT (US) (Effective 2024; replaces the 2023 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Stripe and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2024 version differs from the 2023 version in the following ways: 2024 update revised Connect platform-onboarding obligations, added Stripe Radar/AI-fraud-prevention provisions, refreshed dispute and chargeback handling sections, and updated indemnification and liability caps.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Stripe to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://stripe.com/legal/ssa . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20230101000000*/https://stripe.com/legal/ssa .

This Terms of Service document governs the relationship between you and Shopify, a company that provides e-commerce services. The key provisions are summarized below:

### Service Name
The service covered by these Terms of Service is essentially Shopify's range of e-commerce products and services.

### Key Provisions

* **Scope**: The Terms of Service apply to Shopify's products and services as described on the company's official terms page.
* **User Content and License**: You grant Shopify the right to use your submitted content to operate, improve, and train its AI/ML systems, subject to your settings and applicable laws.
* **Privacy**: Shopify cross-references its published Privacy Policy, which outlines the personal data collected and how it is processed.
* **Dispute Resolution**: Most cases will require **binding arbitration (a private dispute process instead of court)** with class-action waivers, but you have a 30-day opt-out window if you set up a new account.
* **Termination**: Either Shopify or you can terminate the agreement under specified conditions described in the live document.

### Harmful Clauses to Note

* **Arbitration**: The requirement for binding arbitration may be limiting your right to seek redress through the courts. **Be aware of your 30-day opt-out window.**
* **Limited Rights to User Content**: While the Terms of Service allow Shopify to use your content for some purposes, there may be gaps in how your data is used or what rights you retain over it.

### Conclusion

These Terms of Service lay out the ground rules for your relationship with Shopify. Familiarize yourself with the agreements, particularly regarding arbitration, data use, and termination. If you have questions or need help with a specific term, consult Shopify's provided contact information.
source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — SHOPIFY TERMS OF SERVICE (Effective 2024; replaces the 2023 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Shopify and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2024 version differs from the 2023 version in the following ways: 2024 update added Shopify Magic / AI-feature provisions, clarified that merchant store content may be used to power AI features only at the merchant's store level (not for training shared models), and revised payouts and risk-scoring sections.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Shopify to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://www.shopify.com/legal/terms . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20230101000000*/https://www.shopify.com/legal/terms .

**Summary of Wikipedia Term of Use**

These terms apply to your relationship with Wikipedia (also known as the Wikimedia Foundation) and cover its products and services. Wikipedia is a collaborative online encyclopedia, and the Terms of Service are divided into several key sections.

**Scope**: These terms govern your use of Wikipedia and its services. 

**Content and License**: When you upload content to Wikipedia, you grant them the right to use, improve, and train AI/Machine Learning systems using that data, but this is subject to your privacy settings and applicable laws.

**Privacy**: Wikipedia's **Privacy Policy** explains what personal data they collect, how it is used, and how it is processed. This section of the Terms of Service cross-references this policy.

**Termination**: Either you or Wikipedia can terminate the agreement at any time, subject to specific conditions outlined in the current document.

Some potential points of concern for users include:

* **Dispute Resolution**: The Terms of Service require binding arbitration (a private dispute process instead of a court) for disputes between users and Wikipedia, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts.
 

### Key Provisions

* You agree to provide accurate information
* You are responsible for maintaining the confidentiality of your account information
* You agree not to impersonate someone else
* You must not post abusive, harassing, or threatening content
* You must comply with applicable laws

### Rights

Wikipedia reserves the right to:
* Change the terms of service or any additional terms (these changes are effective immediately when updated in the live document).
 
### Important Links

You can find the current version of these terms of service on the Wikimedia website: https://foundation.wikimedia.org/wiki/Policy:Terms_of_Use
If you have questions about these terms, you can also contact the Wikimedia team at: https://foundation.wikimedia.org/wiki/Policy:Terms_of_Use
source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — WIKIMEDIA TERMS OF USE (Effective 2023; replaces the 2014 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Wikipedia (Wikimedia Foundation) and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2023 version differs from the 2014 version in the following ways: Effective June 7, 2023: first major rewrite since 2014. Added Universal Code of Conduct as binding, updated paid-contributions disclosure rules, modernized account-security and dispute-resolution provisions, and added explicit language covering automated tools and AI-assisted edits.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Wikipedia (Wikimedia Foundation) to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://foundation.wikimedia.org/wiki/Policy:Terms_of_Use . The previous version is available at https://foundation.wikimedia.org/wiki/Policy:Terms_of_Use/9_June_2014 .

response:
[DELTA BULLETS]
- The license granted to ChirpSocial for posted content has been expanded to include modification, creation of derivative works, and use for advertising.
- Data retention period has been increased from 18 months to 36 months after account deletion.
- Waiver of the right to participate in class actions has been introduced.
- The notice period before material changes to the Terms has been removed, and users are now expected to accept changes through continued use.
- The scope of the license has changed from "display" to "use, distribute, modify, and create derivative works."

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have been updated, and there are significant changes. Let's break it down:

* Now, when you post content on ChirpSocial, you grant us a license to not only display it, but to also **modify, create derivative works, and use it for advertising**. This changes the scope of the license from just displaying content to a much broader set of uses. 
* The time we keep your account data after you delete your account has also been extended from **18 months to 36 months**. This means your data will be stored with us for a longer period.
* The previous Terms allowed class actions, but now you've **waived the right to participate in any class action**. This means you won't be able to join or participate in any group lawsuits against us. 
* One change you might not like is that the notice period before we make material changes to the Terms has been removed. This means we can update the Terms without sending you a notification **30 days in advance**, and continued use of the service will be considered acceptance of the new Terms.

Regarding new clauses that may harm you: we've added a new clause that gives us a **more lenient** data retention period, which may be considered a reduction in user privacy. Additionally, the updated Terms restrict your ability to participate in class actions, which may not be in your best interest if you're concerned about group lawsuits.

Please note that these are just changes to the Terms of Service. The exact impact will depend on how these changes are enforced and used in practice.

1. ACCOUNT. By creating an account on ChirpSocial you agree to these Terms.
2. CONTENT LICENSE. You grant ChirpSocial a worldwide, perpetual, irrevocable, royalty-free license to use, distribute, modify, and create derivative works from content you post, including for advertising.
3. DATA RETENTION. We retain account data for 36 months after account deletion.
4. ARBITRATION. Disputes are resolved by binding arbitration. You waive the right to participate in any class action.
5. CHANGES. We may modify these Terms at any time. Continued use constitutes acceptance.

response:
[DELTA BULLETS]
- The time period for all sales to be final has changed from 14 days to 7 days.
- Returned items are no longer eligible for a full refund, but only store credit.
- The payment method ShopFast Pay has been added.
- The terms for sharing purchase history with marketing partners have changed: opt-out was previously available, now it's only available for users in the EU, and sharing is no longer conditional on opting out.

[NARRATIVE]
Let's go over the key changes in the updated Terms of Service.

**Changes affecting purchases:**
The time period for all sales to be final has decreased from **14 days** to just **7 days** after delivery. This means that if you want to dispute a purchase, you'll need to act much faster than before. The Terms of Service say: "All sales are final 7 days after delivery." (You might want to review this with your customer support team if you have any issues.)

**Return policy changes:**
Now, **returned items are only eligible for store credit, not a full refund**, even within the 14-day return window. In the previous terms, returns were eligible for a full refund. The Terms of Service say: "Items may be returned within 14 days for store credit only."

**New payment option:**
ShopFast Pay is now an accepted payment method. This might be beneficial if you had trouble using the previous payment options.

**Changes to how we share your purchase history:**
The most significant change in the updated Terms of Service is related to how we share your purchase history with marketing partners. Now, opting out is only available for users in the **EU** (European Union). Previously, users worldwide could opt out of sharing their purchase history. The Terms of Service say: "We share your purchase history with marketing partners. Opt-out is available only for users in the EU."
source_tos:
1. PURCHASES. All sales are final 7 days after delivery.
2. RETURNS. Items may be returned within 14 days for store credit only.
3. SHIPPING. Standard delivery is 5-7 business days.
4. PAYMENT. We accept Visa, MasterCard, PayPal, and ShopFast Pay.
5. PRIVACY. We share your purchase history with marketing partners. Opt-out is available only for users in the EU.
previous_tos:
1. PURCHASES. All sales are final 14 days after delivery.
2. RETURNS. Items may be returned within 14 days for a full refund.
3. SHIPPING. Standard shipping is 5-7 business days.
4. PAYMENT. We accept Visa, MasterCard, and PayPal.
5. PRIVACY. We may share your purchase history with marketing partners unless you opt out.

- Sales-final window shortened from 14 days to 7 days after delivery.

- Default for sharing purchase history is now opt-in by default; opt-out restricted to EU users (was global opt-out).
[CHANGES TO IGNORE]
- Shipping window unchanged (wording 'shipping' vs 'delivery' is cosmetic).
- Visa, MasterCard, PayPal still accepted.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The effective date of the Terms of Service has been updated from 2024 to 2025.
- The Terms of Service now allow users to export some of their data.
- Separate support terms may be governed by a different agreement.
- Some trial-period offers now require auto-renewal to be turned on.
- Non-Microsoft third-party platforms may track and share user data when accessing Xbox Game Studio titles.

[NARRATIVE]
The latest update to the Terms of Service has added a few key points and modified some existing ones. 

Firstly, **the effective date has been updated to 2025**. This means that as of the new date, the updated terms will be in effect. There is no indication that previous agreements made under the 2024 terms will be affected.

Regarding your content, **a new subsection on exportable data has been added**. This now explains what data you can take with you when leaving or terminating the service. This change is likely meant to inform users about their data rights, but it may depend on the specifics of how the clauses are enforced.

In the SUPPORT section, the language has been updated. **Now, it's mentioned that some services may have separate support terms governed outside of this agreement**. While this change affects the way support works for certain services, it doesn't necessarily put users at a disadvantage. However, be aware that support for individual services might be handled differently.

In the PAYMENT section, **some trial-period offers now come with an auto-renewal requirement**. This means users may be automatically enrolled in paid subscriptions. Make sure to carefully review the terms before engaging with these offers to avoid unexpected charges.

Lastly, regarding XBOX, **added language concerns the tracking and sharing of user data by non-Microsoft third-party platforms** when accessing Xbox Game Studio titles. This could potentially affect users' data and their online experience.

On the face of it, none of these changes seem overtly detrimental; however, consider your data handling preferences. If you're using trial-period offers, pay close attention to auto-renewal requirements.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The effective date of the document has changed from 2023 to 2024.
- The moderation rules section no longer describes the rules in text, but instead links to an external Microsoft policy page for more information.
- The Xbox terms now mention that third-party platforms hosting Xbox titles may track and share user data, subject to those platforms' terms.
- Family-settings features may not be available on third-party platforms.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have been updated, and there are some key changes I'd like to highlight for you. 

Firstly, the effective date of the document has changed to 2024. This is more of a housekeeping change, so it doesn't directly affect how you use the services.

Next, the moderation rules section has been updated. Previously, the rules were described in-text, but now the document links to an external Microsoft policy page that describes moderation and enforcement in more detail. This might be a good thing - you'll have a chance to click through and see exactly how the rules are enforced.

Moving on to Xbox-related changes, if you're using third-party platforms to host Xbox titles, the Terms of Service now warn you that those platforms might be tracking and sharing your data, according to their own terms. This is an important change, as you'll need to consider how your data is being used on these third-party platforms.

Lastly, if you're using Xbox services and trying to set up family settings, you should know that these features might not be available on third-party platforms. 

As for any new clauses that may harm you, I'd draw your attention to the fact that you're agreeing to the terms of the third-party platforms, which might include data tracking and sharing. However, it's worth noting that these platforms already have their own terms in place, and the Microsoft service is just informing you of this potential data collection.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The Terms of Service now cover consumer use separately from API and business use.
- The arbitration provider has been changed from ADR Services to National Arbitration and Mediation.
- The procedures for batch arbitration have been revised to align with the new arbitration provider.

[NARRATIVE]
The updated Terms of Service bring a few key changes. One notable change is the way the Terms of Service are structured:

The Terms of Service say that consumer terms are now separated from those covering business and API use. Previously, this document covered both consumer and business/API use. (SCOPE clause)

This update now refers readers to a separate Business Terms document for API and Enterprise use, leaving the current Terms of Service to only cover consumer use.

Regarding arbitration:

The Terms of Service say that the arbitration provider has been changed from ADR Services to National Arbitration and Mediation. Arbitration (a private dispute process instead of court) was previously handled by ADR Services, so this change may mean you will have to go through a new process if you have a dispute.

Additionally, the batch arbitration procedures have been revised to reflect how National Arbitration and Mediation handles such cases. However, since there are no specific details about what this means in practice, without more information, it is difficult to say how this change may impact you.

There are no clauses that stand out as explicitly harming consumers, but some may benefit from being aware of the changes in the arbitration process.

It's always a good idea to review and familiarize yourself with the updated Terms of Service, so you understand your rights and obligations.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The Services Agreement now covers a wider range of business services beyond just API, ChatGPT Enterprise, and ChatGPT Team.
- Business and API customer data is no longer used to train OpenAI's models by default.
- The indemnification language has been updated.
- Service-level commitments have been updated and consolidated.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have undergone some changes. Let's review what's new and what's changed.

One of the primary updates is that the scope of the Services Agreement has been expanded. This means that the agreement now applies to a wider range of business services beyond just API, ChatGPT Enterprise, and ChatGPT Team.

Another significant change is related to data handling. Previously, data-handling provisions varied across different products, but now there's a unified data-handling provision. The key point here is that business and API customer data is no longer used to train OpenAI's models by default.

The indemnification language has also been updated. Without getting into details, it's been consolidated into the new agreement.

Lastly, service-level commitments have been updated and consolidated. This simplifies the agreement and likely clarifies expectations around performance.

As for potential concerns, the updated Terms of Service don't introduce any new obligations that may directly harm you. The changes generally seem to aim at simplifying and consolidating various aspects of the agreement. However, it's always a good idea to review the agreement carefully and reach out to support if you have any specific questions or concerns.

4. SLAs. Service-level commitments updated and consolidated.

- The scope of the Terms now explicitly includes the Claude apps.

**Changes to the Terms of Service:**

The scope of the Terms of Service now explicitly includes the Claude apps, in addition to Claude.ai and Claude Pro. This means that any use of the Claude apps will be covered under these Terms.

The provisions related to "ENTERPRISE LINKING" have been refined. Previously, the language was limited, but now it includes a notice before linking accounts created with employer-owned email domains. This gives you advance notice and a chance to agree to the linking.

The "ACCEPTABLE USE" section now has a stronger reference to the published Acceptable Use Policy. Unfortunately, this means the Terms of Service no longer explain what exactly is and isn't acceptable use, instead referencing the larger policy.

The "DISPUTE RESOLUTION" section has been updated, but the specifics of what changed are not mentioned. This means we can't identify any changes that might harm you.

**New Clauses:**

Nothing stands out as immediately potentially harmful, but keep in mind the stronger reference to the Acceptable Use Policy might mean greater scrutiny of your behavior when using the service. Be sure to read and adhere to the Acceptable Use Policy.

**Key Takeaways:**

* Additional scope to cover the Claude apps
* Refined employer-domain linking process with advance notice
* Stronger reference to the Acceptable Use Policy (check that policy for specifics)

response:
[DELTA BULLETS]
- The opening paragraph now explicitly includes using Meta products as agreement to the Terms.
- You no longer retain exclusive rights to content uploaded to Meta; it may be used, distributed, and modified to improve services.
- Meta's AI/ML systems now use user content not only for service improvement but also for safety.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have been updated, and I'll walk you through the changes.

The opening paragraph now explicitly includes using Meta products as agreement to the Terms. This means that by using our services, you're accepting these Terms, so be sure you understand what's in them.

In terms of your content, a few things have changed. **Previously, worldwide license to display your content was granted, but now it includes using content for distribution and modification to operate and improve services.** This means that Meta may use, distribute, and even modify your content to improve our services. While this clause is quite broad, it's worth noting that it doesn't inherently harm you. On the other hand, **formerly, you retained exclusive rights to your content until it's deleted. Now, Meta mentions that the license for content uploaded to Meta ends when content is deleted, which means we won't use it after that point.**

Regarding AI and machine learning, the old Terms mentioned automated systems in general, while the new Terms explicitly state that Meta will use **AI and machine-learning systems on your user content for both service improvement and safety.**

To summarize, here's what's changed:

* Using Meta products includes accepting the Terms.
* Content uploaded to Meta may be used, distributed, and modified for service improvement.
* Meta's use of AI/ML systems on user content now includes safety as a purpose.

Overall, the changes don't seem particularly detrimental, but it's essential to review these Terms to ensure you're comfortable with the amendments.

The Terms of Service have expanded the license for the content you upload. In the old version, you gave a non-exclusive license to host and display your content. The data-flow provisions have been updated to include explicit information about how data will be shared across Facebook, Instagram, Threads, and Messenger. This means that Instagram may share more data with other Meta Products (Clause 4, CURRENT TERMS OF USE).

Lastly, the Terms of Service have been "aligned with Meta umbrella terms", which might strengthen integration between Instagram and Meta, though the exact impact isn't specified.

While this can lead to better experiences, the exact extent of data collection and analysis isn't specified.
* Explicit data-flow provisions for sharing data across Meta products (Clause 4, CURRENT TERMS OF USE): This could lead to more data being shared between different Meta services.
* Alignment with Meta umbrella terms (Item from the CHANGE SUMMARY): While this might improve the overall Instagram experience, it may also further strengthen Meta's overall data collection practices.

Keep in mind that these are just the changes in the agreement. If you have concerns, it's a good idea to review the full updated Terms of Service.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The scope of the Content License has been expanded to include training machine-learning and generative-AI models.
- Users are no longer given an option to opt out of having their content used for AI training.
- The range of third-party data sharing allowed has been broadened beyond just partner relationships. 
- Twitter / X services is now more specifically referred to as X services.

[NARRATIVE]
Let's review the changes to the Terms of Service.

The main addition is that the **CONTENT LICENSE** now explicitly extends to using your posts to train **machine-learning and generative-AI models**. This means that your content can be used to develop these technologies without your explicit permission.

Regarding **AI TRAINING**, previously, users like you had the option to **opt out** of having their content used for this purpose. However, this **in-product opt-out language** has been **removed** from the Terms of Service. You are no longer explicitly given the choice to opt out.

In terms of **THIRD-PARTY DATA SHARING**, the Terms now permit **broader sharing of content** with third parties, subject to the terms of the license.

Lastly, the **SCOPE** of the Terms has been updated to refer to the X services collectively as "**X services**".

As for clauses that may harm you, note that the explicit option to opt out of AI training has been removed. This might raise concerns about the use of your content without your consent.

Here are the specific points regarding the changes:

* The Content License has been expanded to allow for AI training without user consent.
* The in-product opt-out option has been removed, leaving users without explicit control over their content's use for AI training.
* Third-party data sharing is now broader in scope.
* The service name has been updated to X services.
* This version adds: Worldwide royalty-free license now explicitly extends to using posts to train machine-learning and generative-AI models.
* This version removes: In-product setting allowed users to opt out of having content used for AI training.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The contracting party has been changed from "TikTok Inc." to "TikTok USDS" (after a U.S. joint venture).
- The content license is now irrevocable.
- The content license now includes reaffirmation for ML model development.
- Users are now responsible for the inputs and outputs of AI models.
- Users are prohibited from stripping watermarks from AI outputs and claiming they are human-made.
- There are no changes to data collection, sharing, account termination, dispute resolution, payments, or liability.

[NARRATIVE]
Let's take a look at the updates.

The Terms of Service now say that the contracting party is "TikTok USDS" (after a U.S. joint venture). This means that instead of the previous company, TikTok USDS is now responsible.

Additionally, the content license has changed in a few ways. It is now **irrevocable**, meaning that once you give TikTok the license, you can't take it back. This version also includes a reaffirmation for ML model development, which means your content can be used to improve machine learning models.

One significant change is the new rules for using **Artificial Intelligence (AI)**. Now, you are responsible for the inputs and outputs of AI models, which means if an AI generates something that gets you into trouble, it's your responsibility. You are also not allowed to remove watermarks from AI outputs or claim that they are human-made.

The following changes may be of note:

* **Changes to the contracting party:** It is now "TikTok USDS."
* **Content license updates:**
  * The license is now **irrevocable.**
  * The license includes a reaffirmation for ML model development.
* **New AI rules:**
  + You are responsible for the inputs and outputs of AI models.
  + You are not allowed to remove watermarks from AI outputs or claim they are human-made.

These changes could potentially affect your use of the platform. Keep in mind that you are now contractually responsible for the outputs of AI models, which may impact how you use and interact with AI tools within the platform.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The user can now monetize their videos on YouTube, even without being a Partner creator.
- Facial-recognition data cannot be collected from videos uploaded to the platform.
- Non-U.S. creators receiving payments from YouTube must comply with new U.S. tax-withholding obligations.
- The Terms now apply globally, rather than being region-specific.

[NARRATIVE]
The updated Terms of Service have made some significant changes.

One major change is in **Monetization**. Previously, only YouTube Partner Program creators could monetize their videos, but now non-Partner creators can also do so (point 1 in the current Terms of Service).

Another change is in **Facial Recognition**. A new rule now prohibits collecting facial-recognition data from videos uploaded to YouTube (point 2 in the current Terms of Service). This means you're not allowed to collect or use facial data from your uploaded content.

There's also a change in tax obligations. **Tax** policies for non-U.S. creators receiving payments from YouTube have been updated to include new U.S. tax-withholding obligations (point 3 in the current Terms of Service). This affects non-U.S. creators and may have implications for their finances.

Lastly, the **Scope** of the Terms has been updated to be global, rather than region-specific (point 4 in the current Terms of Service). This means the Terms now apply to all users worldwide, without variations depending on the user's region.

The updated Terms of Service haven't explicitly mentioned any new clauses that would directly harm you, but it's worth noting that you must comply with these changes to avoid any issues. If you have concerns, the most effective way is to review these updates and adjust your behavior on the platform accordingly.

Please let me know if you'd like me to clarify any specific point. If not, I'll be happy to answer any questions you may have.

- Adobe now allows access to user content via both 'automated and manual methods' (previously only mentioned 'narrow service-operation purposes').
- Adobe now explicitly states they do not train generative-AI models on customer cloud content, after previously having a limited or implicit clause.

[NARRATIVE]
Adobe has made updates to the Terms of Service, and we'll go over the key changes.

The most notable change is to **Clause 1: ACCESS**. Initially, this clause allowed Adobe to access your user content via automated and manual methods. This sparked public backlash. Now, the clause still grants Adobe access to your user content, but it mentions both automated and manual methods. **The Terms of Service say that Adobe can access your user content using both automated and manual methods**, whereas previously it said only for narrow service-operation purposes.

Another significant change is to **Clause 2: AI TRAINING**. The updated Terms of Service explicitly state that Adobe **does not train generative-AI models on customer cloud content**. This provides more transparency and addresses concerns from the previous update. **There is now a clear statement that protects your user content from being used for AI training**, whereas the previous clause was limited and implicit.

Additionally, **Adobe has added plain-English summaries of the changes** alongside the standard legal language. This makes the Terms of Service easier to understand, but it doesn't necessarily change the substance.

The language and wording of the sections have also been rewritten to be clearer and easier to understand. While this change doesn't introduce any new harm, it's a positive move towards transparency.

Overall, the changes aim to provide more clarity and transparency regarding Adobe's access to user content. However, it's essential to note that the Terms of Service still grant Adobe access to your user content, which may be a concern for some users.

New provisions or policies that may affect you:

* Adobe has expanded its access to your user content to include automated and manual methods.
* Generative-AI models will not be trained on your customer cloud content.

Keep in mind that, at its core, the Terms of Service define the relationship between you and Adobe. If you're concerned about any of these changes or have specific questions, I suggest carefully reviewing the updated Terms of Service.

- The NEW version permits Zoom to use Service-Generated Data to train AI/ML models, whereas the OLD version did not.
- The NEW version requires customer consent before Zoom can use audio, video, and chat content to train AI models, whereas the OLD version did not have this requirement.
- The CUSTOMER CONTENT section remains unchanged, but its placement and surrounding context changed, leading to this interpretation, whereas the OLD version covered it by privacy commitments.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have been modified to allow Zoom to use Service-Generated Data to train AI/ML models. This broad license was not present in the previous version. Now, Zoom can use data it collects to train its models, which was not the case before.

Additionally, the updated Terms of Service have introduced a new clause that requires customer consent before Zoom can use audio, video, and chat content to train AI models. This is a change from the previous version, which did not have this requirement.

The CUSTOMER CONTENT section is also worth noting, as it now has a different placement and surrounding context. However, the underlying content remains the same, as it is still subject to customer-controlled use.

As for potential harm, we can flag a few points to consider:

* The broad license on Service-Generated Data could be used to benefit Zoom in developing its AI capabilities, but it may also mean that users' data is used without explicit permission.
* The requirement for customer consent before using audio, video, and chat content to train AI models is a positive change as it ensures users have more control over their data.
* The CUSTOMER CONTENT section remains unchanged, meaning users continue to have control over their audio, video, and chat content.

Please note that the Terms of Service do not explicitly mention what happens when a user chooses not to consent to the use of their data. However, the requirement for consent is a positive step towards user autonomy.

response:
[DELTA BULLETS]
- The OLD version explicitly mentioned no AI-training provisions, while the NEW version explicitly states that member data and content may be used for AI training.
- The NEW version introduces an opt-out toggle in Settings for AI training, giving users more control over their data usage.
- The dispute-resolution provisions in the NEW version include a class-action waiver, which is not mentioned in the OLD version.

[NARRATIVE]
The most notable changes involve the use of member data and content for Artificial Intelligence (AI) training. Previously, the Terms of Service did not mention AI training provisions. However, this version explicitly states that member data and content **may be used to train generative-AI models for LinkedIn features**.

This means that LinkedIn has the right to use the data you share on the platform to train AI models, which might be used to enhance their features. However, you now have more control over this: an **opt-out toggle** has been introduced in the Settings to allow users to **choose whether their data is used for AI training**.

Another change involves the dispute-resolution provisions, which have been updated to include a **class-action waiver** (a private dispute process instead of court). This means that if you have a dispute with LinkedIn, you may not be able to join a group lawsuit or class-action case.

In contrast to the OLD version, the NEW version no longer explicitly mentions no AI-training provisions, but instead has an explicit statement about data use, as well as an opt-out option. This gives you the ability to turn off data use for AI training or choose a setting related to this.

1. CONTENT LICENSE. Same baseline license, with explicit reference to use for AI training.
2. AI TRAINING. New explicit clause: member data and content may be used to train generative-AI models for LinkedIn features.
3. SETTINGS. New opt-out toggle in Settings for AI training.
4. DISPUTES. Updated dispute-resolution provisions, including class-action waiver language.

- Worldwide license framing predates this change.

- Clarified that Customer Data is not used to train Slack's generative-AI products.
- Narrowed the previous language about ML use for global model training.
- Added new Slack-AI-specific terms.

[NARRATIVE]
Let's go through the changes to the Terms of Service.

Previous to the update, the policy didn't have specific provisions for Slack's AI products. Now, it does - **Slack-AI-specific terms have been added**.

The way Slack handles Customer Data has been clarified. According to the new Terms of Service, **your Customer Data is not used to train Slack's generative-AI products**.

Additionally, the Terms of Service previously mentioned **Machine Learning (ML) for global model training** without specifying the details. In the latest update, this language has been **narrowed**, but the specifics on what this means are not provided in the document. It's unclear from the information given if the change is beneficial, neutral, or not favorable to you.

The Terms of Service do not address potential harm from these changes. They simply clarify how Slack handles Customer Data and ML. However, without more detail, it's difficult to assess whether the changes might benefit or harm you.

To better understand your rights and options, I recommend reviewing the new Terms of Service carefully or seeking advice from the relevant parties. If you're concerned about the narrowed ML language or Slack-AI-specific terms, consider inquiring with Slack's support team for further clarification.

- The use of Slack data to train large language models without permission is now explicitly prohibited.

Let's go through the changes. 

Previously, the policy was more general when it came to what apps could access your data (APP DATA). Now, there are better-defined data-export limits.

Before, there were already some specific restrictions on bulk extraction by apps (BULK EXTRACTION), but they've been made stricter. This basically means apps can't pull large amounts of your data all at once, even if they're authorized to access it.

Another significant change is the addition of a new clause explicitly prohibiting the use of Slack data to train large language models (LLM USE) without explicit permission from Slack. This clause wasn't present in the previous version.

As for new clauses that may harm you, I've flagged the ones related to LLM USE. This new clause clearly prohibits you from training language models on your Slack data without permission from Slack. However, this is more on a permission level (do you have Slack's permission?) rather than a clause harming your use.

If you're developing an app that interacts with Slack or want to train a language model on Slack data, you'll want to check the clause prohibiting LLM USE. You may need to get permission from Slack before doing so.

service_name: GitHub Terms of Service / Privacy Statement
response:
[DELTA BULLETS]
- Personal data can now be shared with Microsoft and other GitHub affiliates.
- Personal data may be used to develop, improve, and train AI/ML models, in addition to security and operational purposes.
- User opt-out preferences and enterprise data protections no longer apply when data is shared with affiliates.

[NARRATIVE]
Let's go through the updates. 

One of the main changes is the way GitHub shares your personal data with affiliates. Previously, personal data was only shared with affiliates for limited operational purposes. Now, it can be shared with Microsoft and other GitHub affiliates for AI/ML model development (making software smarter using computer learning).

This means your personal data may be used in ways it wasn't before, such as training machine learning models. 

Another change is the expansion of the purposes for processing your personal data. While the list of purposes was previously standard and mostly operational, it now includes developing, improving, and training AI/ML models.

A possible concern is the introduction of new AI/ML-related data processing purposes, which may involve using your personal data without explicit consent for improving AI/ML models.

Regarding opt-outs, previously, user preferences and enterprise data protections would travel with the data when shared with affiliates. However, now these protections do not apply when your data is shared with affiliates.

The changes suggest that more of your data may be shared with affiliates, potentially without your consent or opt-out preferences being applied when data is shared.

**New clauses that may be of concern:**

* Personal data being shared with Microsoft and other GitHub affiliates for AI/ML model development (clause 1 under AFFILIATES)
* Using personal data to develop, improve, and train AI/ML models (clause 3 under AI/ML)
* User opt-out preferences and enterprise data protections not applying when data is shared with affiliates (clause 4 under OPT-OUTS)

1. AFFILIATES. Personal data may now be shared with Microsoft and other GitHub affiliates for AI/ML model development.

3. AI/ML. Explicit purpose for using personal data to develop, improve, and train AI/ML models.
4. OPT-OUTS. User opt-out preferences and enterprise data protections travel with the data when shared with affiliates.

response:
[DELTA BULLETS]
- The company now has the rights to process user-uploaded audio and podcasts with artificial intelligence, which wasn't previously specified.
- Rules have been introduced for AI-generated playlists and an AI-DJ feature that didn't exist before.
- Dispute resolution and class-action waiver clauses have been updated, but specifics about the changes are not provided. 
- Arbitration is still enforced for disputes, but the manner in which they're resolved has been updated.

[NARRATIVE]
This version adds some updates that are worth noting. The most significant change is related to user-uploaded content. Previously, the license only covered standard user-uploaded podcasts and other audio; now it has been expanded to include **AI processing of uploaded audio and podcasts**.

Another key change is the introduction of new rules for **AI-generated playlists** and the **AI DJ feature**. This means that when you use these features, the Terms of Service will apply to the AI-generated content.

Lastly, the dispute resolution clause has been updated. **Binding arbitration (a private dispute process instead of court)** is still a requirement, but the exact manner in which disputes are resolved has changed. Class-action waiver clauses have also been updated.

As it stands, there are no obvious clauses that may harm you directly in the updated Terms of Service, but it's essential to understand these changes to be aware of how they might impact your use of Spotify.

**Changes and their corresponding clauses in the updated Terms of Service:**

- **New clause 1: USER CONTENT** now covers AI processing of uploaded audio and podcasts.
- **New clause 2: AI** introduces rules for AI-generated playlists and AI-dj features.
- **Updated dispute resolution clause** in DISPUTES now includes updated arbitration and class-action waiver clauses.

1. USER CONTENT. License expanded to cover AI processing of uploaded audio and podcasts.
2. AI. Added rules for AI DJ and AI-generated playlists.
3. DISPUTES. Updated arbitration and class-action waiver clauses.

1. USER CONTENT. Standard license over user-uploaded podcasts and other audio.
2. AI. No AI-DJ or AI-playlist provisions.
3. DISPUTES. Standard arbitration clauses.

- User-Content license expanded to cover AI processing of uploaded audio/podcasts.

- Spotify continued to license user content for service operation across both versions.

response:
[DELTA BULLETS]
- The practice of account sharing across households is no longer tolerated.
- The 'Netflix Household' term is now explicitly defined.
- A paid extra-member fee is now charged for users outside the primary household.
- The company has made changes to its billing and cancellation provisions.
- Account sharing is only allowed with paid additional members, not free.

[NARRATIVE]
Let's take a look at what's changed.

The practice of sharing your account with households outside of your primary household is no longer tolerated. This means if you have friends or family members using your account who don't live with you, you'll need to get a paid additional member account for them.

A new concept called "Netflix Household" is now explicitly defined, but the Terms of Service don't explain what this means exactly. However, they do explain that a paid extra-member fee is now charged for users outside the primary household.

The billing and cancellation provisions have been updated, but the exact changes aren't specified in the text.

As for potentially harming you, here are some key points to consider:

* Paid sharing now requires additional members from outside your household, and you'll be charged for them.
* Sharing your account indiscriminately is no longer allowed.
* Although not mentioned, you might risk having your account suspended or terminated if you're found to be sharing your account with non-paid members outside your household.

To be clear, I'm not saying these rules will necessarily harm you; I'm just highlighting what's changed. If you're unsure about how these updates affect you, I recommend reviewing the updated Terms of Service or reaching out to Netflix directly for assistance.

- The scope of the Terms of Service has been broadened to include Alexa, Rufus AI, and other AI services.

- Users now retain the right to go to small-claims court for disputes (previously arbitration was binding).

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have undergone some changes. Here's a summary of what's new:

The scope of the Terms of Service has been broadened to include services like Alexa and Rufus AI, in addition to the existing Amazon services. This means that these services are now subject to these Terms of Service.

The Terms of Service now have specific references to AI-generated outputs and how they interact with the user agreement. However, these references don't indicate any specific changes that could harm you.

Regarding arbitration, the Terms of Service now include an explicit small-claims-court carve-out, meaning that you still have the right to take disputes to small-claims court, rather than being forced into binding arbitration.

It's worth noting that arbitration (a private dispute process instead of court) now has some limitations, but these limitations don't seem particularly burdensome. However, the carve-out for small-claims court is a positive change for users.

Overall, these changes seem to clarify the scope of the Terms of Service and provide additional guidance on AI-generated outputs, without introducing any clearly problematic clauses.

New clause flagged: None

Note: Remember that the Terms of Service are a general agreement, not a specific set of rules for every situation. If you have a specific concern, it's best to review the Terms of Service page in context.

response:
[DELTA BULLETS]
- End-to-end encryption is now optional (previously standard encryption-at-rest).
- Apple's access for legal/safety reasons is narrowed where end-to-end encryption applies.
- Apple's server-side AI ("Apple Intelligence Private Cloud Compute") is now acknowledged.
- Users can opt-in to advanced end-to-end encryption for select iCloud data categories.

[NARRATIVE]
Let's take a look at what's changed. The most notable change is that **end-to-end encryption is now optional** for some iCloud data categories. Previously, encryption was standard, but now users can opt-in to more robust encryption. This adds an extra layer of protection for your data.

Additionally, **Apple's access for legal/safety reasons is now narrower** in situations where end-to-end encryption is used. This means that in cases where your data is encrypted from end-to-end, Apple will have limited access to it, which helps maintain your privacy.

Another change is the introduction of **Apple Intelligence Private Cloud Compute**, which is Apple's server-side AI technology that's designed to provide more personalized services while preserving your privacy. However, this adds a new level of data processing to the service.

The following changes were highlighted:

* **Added Advanced Data Protection**: The Terms of Service now include separate data protection mechanisms for users who opt-in to end-to-end encryption. Advanced Data Protection preserves your right to access your data until you decide to use it with end-to-end encryption; whereas standard encryption disables user access to their data before turning encryption on.
* **No red flags.** However we can point out some features that may require your attention:
  * The Terms of Service don't mention your right to opt-out of the Advanced Data Protection mechanism
  * Opting into Advanced Data Protection changes your data encryption protocol. The Terms of Service do not describe how opting-in, and opting-out works, or what are the implications for your data.

2. ACCESS. Apple's access for legal/safety reasons clarified, narrowed where end-to-end encryption applies.

One key change is in the handling of **customer data**. The previous version of the Terms didn't specifically address how your data might be used in relation to our AI features. However, the original wording raised concerns about using your data to train our AI models.

To address these concerns, the new Terms explicitly state that your customer data will **not be used to train third-party AI models without your consent**. This provides more transparency and control over how your data is shared and used.

Overall, these changes aim to improve your experience with our service while protecting your data and ensuring that you have a clear understanding of how your information is used.

Note that the Terms don't explicitly mention any new clauses that harm you. However, the new AI-related features may have additional consequences or implications that aren't immediately clear. If you have specific concerns, please let me know.

- Users now own outputs of Canva's generative-AI tools, but with restrictions (change from no restrictions).
- Canva users are prohibited from training other AI models using Canva-generated content (NEW restriction).
- AI-generated content is subject to additional moderation and labeling requirements (NEW requirement).

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have been updated to reflect some changes in the use of Canva's generative-AI tools. Let's break it down:

**Output Ownership**: Previously, the ownership rules for designs were standard. Now, users own the outputs of Canva's generative-AI tools (specifically, Magic Studio), but it's subject to platform rights. This means you still own the content you create, but the platform has some rights over it too. The actual text doesn't specify what those rights are, but they might be worth exploring if you're concerned about ownership.

**AI Usage**: There's a new restriction on using Canva-generated content to train other AI models. This means you're not allowed to use the content created by Canva's generative-AI tools to train other AI models. This might be a new issue for developers and AI researchers, but it's worth noting that this is a change that specifically affects AI usage.

**Content Moderation**: Additionally, there are new requirements for moderate content, which now includes AI-generated content. This means that AI-generated content will be subject to additional moderation and labeling requirements.

As for any new clauses that may harm you, these are the two main changes:

* Using Canva-generated content to train other AI models is now prohibited.
* AI-generated content is subject to additional moderation and labeling requirements.

These changes primarily affect users of Canva's generative-AI tools, particularly developers and AI researchers. The actual text doesn't specify any particular harm to users, but it's essential to be aware of these changes to avoid any potential issues.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- Notion AI will now take ownership of input data and output data generated by its AI features.
- By default, Notion will not train its foundational models on customer data.
- Enterprise plan users now have data-residency options in their plans.

[NARRATIVE]
Based on the updated Terms of Service, here's a summary of what changed:

Notion has added new provisions related to AI, subprocessors, and enterprise plans.

* Previously, the standard list of subprocessors was not updated. Now, the subprocessor list is updated (clause: 1. SUBPROCESSORS).
* Notion AI has been introduced, which brings changes in terms of ownership, training, and interaction with customer data:
  * Notion AI will now take ownership of the input data you provide and the output data generated by its AI features (New clause: AI and input/output ownership). 
    * As a result, you may lose control over the data used to train AI models or the data produced by these models (Potential issue).
  * By default, Notion will not train its foundational models on customer data (New clause: AI and no training of foundational models), but it's unclear if this applies to data imported from other sources or external integrations.
* Enterprise plan features have been updated:
  * Enterprise plan users now have data-residency options in their plans, enabling them to choose where their data is stored (New clause: ENTERPRISE and data-residency options).

Overall, these updates seem to be improving the user experience for Enterprise users. However, the introduction of Notion AI and its data ownership provisions could potentially impact how you interact with your data and the level of control you have over it.

As always, you can re-evaluate the Terms of Service and decide if these updates align with your expectations and usage of Notion. Keep in mind that these changes are part of an ongoing update cycle, and future changes may affect how you use Notion's features.

Moving on to the CUSTOMER FILES section, a key change has been made. The previous version simply contained standard confidentiality language. Now, the new Terms of Service specify that customer file content will not be used to train third-party generative models without your explicit opt-in. 

While these changes do bring transparency, we must consider the potential benefits and consequences of these policy changes.

- The strengthening of security and incident-notification language seems to be purely a positive development.

Overall, the changes appear to primarily focus on introducing transparency and protecting user data. There do not appear to be any new clauses that may directly harm you at this time.

However, the Terms of Service do not address matters like data transfer between other platforms/service providers, or data storage terms, so you might want to review those as well.

Please note that the changes regarding third-party generative models and customer file content opt-in require careful evaluation in the context of using Figma's new features. 

It is also crucial to be aware that the Terms of Service may be interpreted in various ways and might not account for all specific situations. If any aspects of the updated Terms of Service cause you concern, it is advisable to review them in detail and reach out to support (if necessary) for further clarification.

- Adds Poe to the list of covered platforms.
- Allows Poe prompts and responses to be used for improving Poe and partner models, but gives users settings to opt-out.
- Introduces terms for bot developers, which previously did not exist.
- Updates the dispute-resolution provisions, but the specific changes are not detailed here.

[NARRATIVE]
The updated Terms of Service bring some changes that are worth discussing.

Firstly, the scope of what the Terms of Service cover has expanded to include Poe, in addition to Quora. This means that any actions you take on both platforms are subject to these rules.

Regarding Poe specifically, there's a new rule about using Poe prompts and responses to improve Poe and partner models. The important thing to note here is that you have settings to opt-out of this use, if you want to.

Another significant change is the introduction of terms for bot developers. This section applies to anyone who develops bots, and it's likely aimed at providing clear guidelines for how bots should interact with the platforms.

Lastly, the dispute-resolution provisions have been updated. Unfortunately, the updated Terms of Service don't provide enough detail about these changes, so it's hard to say exactly how they may impact you.

Some new clauses to flag as potentially impacting your experience are:
* The updated Terms of Service now apply to both Quora and Poe, which may affect how you use both platforms.
* The opt-out option for using Poe prompts and responses could be beneficial if you're concerned about data use.

Please keep in mind that these are just potential implications based on the changes outlined in the updated Terms of Service. If you have specific concerns, it might be a good idea to revisit this information and consider reaching out if needed.

- Mandatory-arbitration clause has been added (no arbitration previously mentioned).

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have been updated, and there are some key changes to note. 

One major change is the addition of a mandatory-arbitration clause (a private dispute process instead of court). This means that if you have a dispute with us, you'll have to resolve it through arbitration rather than going to court.

Additionally, the dispute-notice window has been shortened, which means you'll have less time to notify us of a dispute before arbitration begins. 

Another change limits your rights to participate in class actions (a lawsuit involving many people with similar claims). This means you won't be able to join a class-action lawsuit against us as easily as you could before.

A new 30-day opt-out window for the new arbitration terms has been introduced, which could be beneficial if you're not happy with the changes. However, if you're automatically opted-in, you should review the terms carefully and consider opting out within the next 30 days if you don't like the changes.

These changes were introduced shortly after the October 2023 data breach, which may be concerning for users who care about data security.

Note these changes and see if they align with your expectations when using our service.

As for potential changes that may harm you:

**No new clauses that may harm you:**

Overall, the changes to the Terms of Service aim to give you more choices and flexibility when resolving disputes with the service.

- **Account Security**: The account-security provisions have been modernized, but the specific changes are not outlined in these changes. However, modernizing the provisions might generally mean you should be more careful about protecting your account.

response:
The arbitration clause does stand out. Specifically, it requires individuals to waive their right to a jury trial and to participate in any class action. This is because they are agreeing to binding arbitration administered by the American Arbitration Association. This means that any disputes arising from the terms would be resolved through a private process, rather than through a court of law (jury trial). Additionally, it means that individual users would not be able to join a group lawsuit (class action) against ChirpSocial. 

It's worth noting that clauses like this are not unheard of, but they can be noteworthy.
source_tos:
1. ACCOUNT. By creating an account on ChirpSocial you agree to these Terms.
2. CONTENT LICENSE. You grant ChirpSocial a worldwide, perpetual, irrevocable, royalty-free license to use, reproduce, distribute, modify, and create derivative works from any content you post, including for advertising and resale to third parties.
3. ARBITRATION. Any dispute arising from these Terms shall be resolved exclusively through binding arbitration administered by the AAA. You waive your right to a jury trial and to participate in any class action.
4. ACCOUNT TERMINATION. We may suspend or terminate your account at any time, for any reason, without prior notice.
5. CHANGES TO TERMS. We may modify these Terms at any time. Continued use after changes constitutes acceptance.
6. SUPPORT. We aim to respond to support tickets within 5 business days.

user_input: Does Steam still require disputes to go to arbitration?

However, there is a note that most updated terms (across the industry) still require binding arbitration with class-action waivers. But Steam's (Valve's) 2024 update actually removed this mandatory arbitration clause, allowing disputes to be resolved through the courts instead.

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Steam (Valve) and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2024 version differs from the 2023 version in the following ways: September 26, 2024 update removed the mandatory arbitration / class-action waiver clauses entirely - Valve now requires disputes to be filed in court (subject to venue rules), reversing several years of arbitration-only language.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Steam (Valve) to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.

user_input: Can I still get an ad-free Disney+ tier?
response:
The Terms of Service say that streaming titles may now show ads even on 'no ads'/'ad free' tiers. This change was made for new subscribers on January 27, 2025, and for existing subscribers on March 24, 2025.

So, it appears that the ad-free option is no longer available.
source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — DISNEY+ SUBSCRIBER AGREEMENT (Effective 2025; replaces the 2024 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Disney+ and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2025 version differs from the 2024 version in the following ways: Effective January 27, 2025 for new subscribers and March 24, 2025 for existing ones: streaming titles may now show ads even on 'no ads'/'ad free' tiers, expanded arbitration with mass-arbitration procedures following Disney's earlier 2024 Wrongful-Death-case controversy, and updated content-availability language.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Disney+ to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://www.disneyplus.com/legal/subscriber-agreement . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20240101000000*/https://www.disneyplus.com/legal/subscriber-agreement .

[REFERENCE ANSWER]
Under the updated Subscriber Agreement (effective January 27, 2025 for new subscribers and March 24, 2025 for existing ones), the 'no ads' / 'ad-free' tiers may now include ads on certain streaming titles at Disney's discretion. So while the tier name remains, true ad-free playback is no longer guaranteed for all content.

- may include ads
- no ads
- no longer guaranteed
